t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we will learn the toxicological examination of cannabis physical evidence. Hashish is a resin secreted from the flowers of Indian hemp and containing the active narcotic component tetrahydrocannabinol, that is THC. The aim of the session is to detect cannabinoids by colour reactions and to confirm THC by chromatography. The plan has four stages. First, preparing an alcoholic extract. Second, the Pauly, Fast Blue B, Duquenois and Buke reactions. Third, paper and thin-layer chromatography. Fourth, interpreting the result.

By the end of the session you should achieve four results. First, detect cannabinoids in the alcoholic extract by colour reactions on filter paper; the sensitivity of these reactions is 1 μg. Second, distinguish cannabidiol, cannabinol and THC in paper chromatography by Rf value and colour, as given in Table 4. Third, confirm THC in thin-layer chromatography by Rf1 and spot colour, as in Table 5. Fourth, evaluate the result correctly. Remember: without detecting THC, no conclusion is drawn that it is cannabis.

Now the reagents and equipment. For the extract, 1 g of sample and 10 ml of 96% alcohol are taken, the extract is applied to filter paper and the reagents are sprayed on. There are four reagents: Pauly reagent, that is 0.05% diazotised sulphanilic acid in 10% Na2CO3, then 0.05% Fast Blue B, and the Duquenois and Buke reagents. For paper chromatography, grade "S" paper 3x30 cm and dimethylformamide with cyclohexane in the ratio 1:5 are used. In thin-layer chromatography, a KSK silica gel plate is used; it is activated at 110 °C for 30 minutes. As the reference, an alcoholic cannabis extract containing THC is taken.

Pay attention to the safety rules. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask to the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard; after the work these rooms are locked and sealed. One more important point: objects from infectious persons, for example those with tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container, and this is noted in the documents. That is, the biological hazard is taken into account in advance.

Cannabis is known by the names hashish, marijuana, plan and bhang, and under the UN convention it is regarded as a narcotic drug. Hashish oil is a thick extract, and it is appropriate to keep it in alcohol or sesame oil. Marijuana contains more than 70 cannabinoids. The table shows the THC content. In marijuana it is 13-15%, in hashish about 2-10%, and in hashish oil 10-60%. Thus the amount of biologically active substances differs sharply according to the type of product.

Let us look at the types of cannabis products. Marijuana consists of the leaves, flowers and fruits from the upper part of the plant. Hashish is in a liquid, waxy state, greenish or dark in colour. Hashish oil is a thick extract kept in alcohol or sesame oil. Besides these, other names are also used: plan, bhang, kif, khusus, charas and dagga. That is, products of different appearance obtained from one plant may be called by different names.

Cannabis constantly contains mainly cannabinol, cannabidiol and tetrahydrocannabinol. But not all three of these substances have a narcotic effect. Of them, only tetrahydrocannabinol has a narcotic effect. Therefore the narcotic property of a sample is confirmed precisely by detecting THC. The basic logic of this analysis: finding cannabinol or cannabidiol is not enough; the decisive substance is THC.

Let us remember a few numbers connected with cannabis. Dried marijuana contains about 400 chemical compounds, and smoke from smoking may contain up to 2000 substances. Marijuana contains more than 70 cannabinoids. For smoking, 500-750 mg is added to tobacco. After consumption the effect begins after 15-30 minutes. These data show that cannabis is a mixture of complex composition.

Let us compare the cannabinoids. Cannabinol, cannabidiol and tetrahydrocannabinol are constantly found in cannabis. Cannabinol and cannabidiol have no narcotic effect. Tetrahydrocannabinol, that is THC, alone has a narcotic effect, so it is the main target of the analysis. Chemically, cannabis consists of dibenzopyran derivatives with a phenolic functional group. Remember: all three substances occur together, but their importance is not the same.

In analysing physical evidence, answers are sought to several questions. First, what does the product consist of, and does it contain parts of the hemp plant? Second, does the product under examination have a narcotic effect? Third, is the product not of the same origin as an authentic sample of cannabis? The order is as follows: first a morphological examination is carried out, then the cannabinoids are detected by chemical reactions.

Now the metabolism of cannabinoids. When smoked, within 5-30 minutes cannabinoids and 9-THC reach a high level in the blood, then fall rapidly. When taken by other routes, the duration of effect is 1.5-3 hours. Cannabinoids are metabolised mainly in the liver. Within five days 80-90% is eliminated: 20% in the urine, 80% in the faeces. This information helps in understanding when biological samples should be taken.

Let us sum up the numbers once more. When smoked, cannabinoids and 9-THC reach a high level in the blood within 5-30 minutes, then fall rapidly. When taken by other routes, the duration of effect is 1.5-3 hours. Cannabinoids are metabolised in the liver, and within five days 80-90% is eliminated. That is, the elimination period is 5 days, and the proportion eliminated is 80-90%.

Cannabis intoxication consists of two phases. The first phase is excitation: lightness, laughter, distraction of attention, racing thoughts. The second phase is depression: colours dim, thinking is inhibited, fear appears. Acute intoxication lasts 1-3 hours and ends in heavy sleep and weakness. When a large amount is taken, psychosis may be observed.

The procedure for isolating cannabinoids is as follows. 10 ml of 96% alcohol is added to 1 g of the sample under test and mixed thoroughly. The mixture is left to soak for 1 hour, then filtered and tested for cannabinoids. The extract is then applied to filter paper as a spot. After drying, the reagents are sprayed on it. This sequence is the general basis for all the colour reactions.

t: Pauly and Fast Blue B reactions
n: Let us look at the Pauly and Fast Blue B reactions. Pauly reagent is a mixture of 0.05% diazotised sulphanilic acid in 10% sodium carbonate solution. Fast Blue B is a 0.05% solution prepared in 10% sodium carbonate or in 1 M sodium hydroxide solution. If cannabinoids are present, a red-pink colour forms first, then bluish, and finally dark pink. The sensitivity of the reaction is 1 μg.

Carrying out the Pauly reaction. The alcoholic extract is applied to filter paper as a spot and dried, then freshly prepared Pauly reagent is sprayed on. If cannabinoids are present, the colour changes in stages: first red-pink, then bluish, finally dark pink. A coloured spot results. The sensitivity of the reaction is 1 μg.

The Duquenois reaction. The reagent is prepared as follows: 2 g of vanillin is dissolved in 100 ml of a 1% solution of acetaldehyde in alcohol. Then 0.2 g of sample is shaken in a test tube with 2 ml of reagent for 1 minute, after which 1 ml of concentrated HCl is added. A pink colour forms first, then blue, then dark pink. Sensitivity 1 μg.

Scheme of the Duquenois reaction. Reagent: 2 g of vanillin is dissolved in 100 ml of a 1% solution of acetaldehyde in alcohol. 2 ml of reagent is added to 0.2 g of sample and shaken for 1 minute, then 1 ml of concentrated HCl is added. A coloured compound forms: first pink, blue, then dark pink. Sensitivity 1 μg.

The Buke reaction. Buke reagent consists of a mixture of 2 parts concentrated sulphuric acid and 3 parts 96% ethyl alcohol. To prepare the sample, 1 g of sample is extracted 3 times with ethyl acetate, 5 ml each time, decolourised with activated charcoal and evaporated. The residue is dissolved in 1 ml of acetone, and 0.5 ml of fresh Buke reagent is added. If cannabinoids are present, a red-brown colour forms.

Let us remember the Buke reaction step by step. First, extraction: 1 g of sample is extracted 3 times with 5 ml of ethyl acetate. Second, purification: the extract is shaken with activated charcoal. Third, it is evaporated in a porcelain dish. Fourth, the residue is dissolved in 1 ml of acetone. Fifth, 0.5 ml of fresh Buke reagent is added. A red-brown colour results; sensitivity 1 μg.

Let us sum up the composition of the reagents. Pauly reagent is 0.05% diazotised sulphanilic acid, prepared in 10% Na2CO3; Fast Blue B is a 0.05% solution. Duquenois reagent: 2 g of vanillin in 100 ml of 1% alcoholic acetaldehyde solution. Buke reagent: a mixture of 2 parts concentrated H2SO4 and 3 parts 96% ethyl alcohol. Knowing the exact composition of the reagents is important for the correctness of the result.

t: Evaluating the result of colour reactions
n: How do we evaluate the result of the colour reactions? The important point is that these reactions are not specific for cannabis: cannabis plants that contain no THC, and other cannabinoids, also give the same colour. If the reactions are negative, no further testing is needed, because the sample does not contain cannabis. If positive, paper, thin-layer and gas-liquid chromatography are carried out to decide whether THC is present.

Let us compare the colour reactions. The colour given with Pauly and Fast Blue B: red-pink, bluish, dark pink. In the Duquenois reaction: pink, blue, dark pink. In the Buke reaction a red-brown colour forms. The sensitivity of all four reactions is the same, that is 1 μg. The difference is only in the colour formed.

Preparing the "reference" solution. Cannabinoids are difficult to isolate individually and they are unstable, so a variety of cannabis containing THC is used as the "reference". 1 g of active cannabis is soaked in 10 ml of 96% alcohol for 24 hours at room temperature, filtered and made up to 10 ml with alcohol. The solution is kept in a hermetically sealed brown container in a refrigerator. It can be used for three months.

Paper chromatography. The strip is prepared from grade "S" paper, 3x30 cm. Phases: freshly distilled dimethylformamide and cyclohexane in the ratio 1:5, shaken for 3 minutes. Cyclohexane saturated with dimethylformamide serves as the mobile phase; the paper is impregnated with dimethylformamide saturated with cyclohexane and dried. The phase is run in the chamber for 250 mm. Then the paper is dried at 60 °C and Pauly or Fast Blue B is sprayed on.

Table 4 gives the results of paper chromatography. Cannabidiol: Rf 0.21, colour yellowish-pink. Cannabinol: Rf 0.56, colour red-pink. THC: Rf 0.83, colour violet. With Pauly reagent, cannabidiol gives a light yellow colour, cannabinol yellow, THC dark yellow. The Rf values are given with an accuracy of ±0.05. Most important: THC gives the highest Rf and a violet spot.

Thin-layer chromatography. The plate is saturated with dimethylformamide and benzene in the ratio 1:1 and dried for 20 minutes; the sample and the reference are spotted on the start line. In a chamber saturated with cyclohexane, when the solvent has risen 15 cm, the plate is removed and dried for 20 minutes. Because cannabinoids move slowly, the plate is chromatographed once more in cyclohexane until it has risen 15 cm. Finally Pauly or Fast Blue B is sprayed on. Since chromatography is carried out twice, the value is designated Rf1.

Table 5 gives the results of thin-layer chromatography; the KSK column is given below. Cannabidiolic acid Rf1 0.13, cannabidiol 0.41, cannabinol 0.75, THC 0.91. On silicic acid sorbent the Rf1 of THC = 0.98, and on KSK 0.91. With Pauly reagent, THC gives a dark yellow, cannabinol a yellow, and cannabidiol a light yellow colour. Thus THC is distinguished from the other cannabinoids by the highest Rf1 value.

Let us compare the Rf1 values on the two sorbents. For cannabidiolic acid, 0.14 on the silicic acid sorbent and 0.13 on KSK. For cannabidiol 0.32 and 0.41. For cannabinol 0.75 and 0.75. For tetrahydrocannabinol 0.98 and 0.91. That is, THC shows the highest Rf1 on both sorbents.

Gas-liquid chromatography, abbreviated GLC. With this method the composition and quantity of cannabinoids are determined. Column 2000x4 mm, methylsilicone elastomer SE-30 3%. Column temperature 212 °C, vaporiser and detector temperature 250 °C. The detector is flame-ionisation; the analytical sample is 10 microlitres. The quantity is determined by the internal standard method, with cocaine hydrochloride used as the internal standard.

Pharmacological examination. If chemical and physicochemical methods do not give sufficient results, pharmacological control may be carried out. It is carried out by physician-pharmacologists and physician-toxicologists. In the method, 2 g of cannabis is burned in a 70 l chamber and animals are kept there for 30 minutes. Excitation, mydriasis, salivation and immobility lasting up to 2 hours are expected.

t: History of cannabis use and legal status
n: History of cannabis use and legal status. In 1942 in the USA the use of preparations from hemp in medicine was permitted, and they were included in the Pharmacopoeia. By 1992 marijuana had been included in the list of controlled narcotic drugs. In the Republic of Uzbekistan it is included in the list of narcotic drugs, and its use is prohibited.

Samples taken to detect cannabis use. In a smoker, a cannabis deposit remains in the oral cavity, on the lips, on the fingers and on the palm. The hands are wiped with a cotton or gauze swab moistened with alcohol. In addition, saliva and a rinse with 50 ml of 70% alcohol saturated with table salt are taken. The swabs, saliva and rinse are sent to the toxicology laboratory in separate containers.

t: Isolation from swabs and saliva analysis
n: Isolation from swabs and analysis of saliva. The cotton or gauze is extracted with 5 ml of diethyl ether twice, 1 minute each time; the ether is evaporated to 0.5-1 ml. To the mixture of 10 ml of saliva and rinse, 10 ml of saturated NaCl is added and it is extracted with 5 ml of ether twice, 5 minutes each. The ether portions are passed through 2 g of anhydrous Na2SO4, evaporated to 0.5 ml and examined by TLC.

t: Preparing saliva and rinse for analysis: the numbers
n: The numbers for preparing saliva and rinse for analysis. From the suspected person, 10 ml of saliva and a rinse with 70% alcohol saturated with table salt, 50 ml, are taken. To 10 ml of the mixture, 10 ml of saturated NaCl is added and it is extracted twice for 5 minutes with 5 ml of diethyl ether. The ether is passed through 2 g of anhydrous Na2SO4, evaporated to 0.5 ml and examined by TLC.

Three rules are followed in interpreting the result. First, without detecting THC or without a pharmacological test, no conclusion can be drawn that it is cannabis. Second, finding cannabinoids only on a swab from the hands cannot be the basis for concluding that the person smoked cannabis. Third, if THC is detected in the saliva and the rinse, it can be concluded that the person smoked cannabis.

Case task. The saliva of a person suspected of drug use and an alcohol swab from his fingers were brought as the object. Question: for which substances must the analysis be carried out? Set out the solution. The direction is as follows: the swabs are tested with colour reactions and TLC, while the saliva and the rinse are analysed separately.

Let us summarise. In the alcoholic extract of cannabis, the Pauly, Fast Blue B, Duquenois and Buke reactions indicate cannabinoids, but they are not specific. THC is identified in paper and thin-layer chromatography by Rf and colour, and in GLC with an internal standard. The conclusion rests on the detection of THC. The report states the object, the method, and the Rf values and colours.
